decisions.claim: B is a student who pays tuition
decisions.reason: Turn 3 is a question from A to B about whether B has a scholarship. Questions do not establish their answers. B might not pay tuition at all (e.g., family pays, or B is not a student). The claim that B 'pays tuition' is not presupposed by the question—A asks if B has a scholarship or is 'on your own,' which is about funding source, not necessarily about B personally paying.
decisions.counterexample: B could be a student whose family pays tuition, or B might not be a student at all and the question was poorly framed.

decisions.claim: B exchanges foreign money into dollars
decisions.reason: Turn 7 says 'changing foreign money into dollars is heart-breaking. You seem to get so little in return.' The 'You seem to get so little in return' is A's general observation about exchange rates, not a confirmed fact that B personally exchanges foreign money. A is making a general statement about currency exchange difficulty. B might not exchange money themselves (family could handle it, or B might not be involved in exchanges).
decisions.counterexample: B's family could be handling the money exchange on B's behalf, or B might receive dollars directly without exchanging.

decisions.claim: B is a student at some educational institution
decisions.reason: Turn 3 'Have you got a scholarship, or are you on your own?' presupposes that B is enrolled in an educational institution where a scholarship would be relevant. This is a necessary presupposition of the question—asking about a scholarship implies the addressee is a student.
decisions.counterexample: It would be very unusual to ask about a scholarship to someone not in an educational institution, but not strictly impossible if A is mistaken.

decisions.claim: B is a foreign national (not from a dollar-using country)
decisions.reason: Turn 7 states 'changing foreign money into dollars is heart-breaking. You seem to get so little in return.' The 'You seem to get so little in return' is directed at B, implying B is the one experiencing this exchange. This presupposes B has foreign money (i.e., is from a non-dollar country or deals in foreign currency), making B a foreign national relative to the dollar-using context.
decisions.counterexample: B could be a dollar-country resident who simply travels and exchanges money, but the framing strongly implies B's home currency is foreign to dollars.

design: dual route, targeted rescue, globally grouped evidence adjudication
